sections.title: The Philistines Plan the Ark’s Return
sections.summary: After seven months the Philistine priests and diviners advise sending the ark back with golden images of tumors and rats as a trespass offering. They set a test: if untrained milk cows carry it toward Beth Shemesh, the God of Israel has done this great evil to them.

groups.title: The Philistines Plan the Ark’s Return

items.title: True Words, Wrong Guidance
items.html: The Philistine priests and diviners said several true things. They knew that guilt must be answered (v. 3). They told their people to give glory to the God of Israel (v. 5). They remembered Pharaoh’s hard heart and warned against repeating it (v. 6). In some ways they remembered the exodus better than Israel had in chapter 4. Yet the same advisers prescribed golden images of tumors and rats, promised healing God had not promised, and set up a test by divination. True observations were mixed with guidance God never gave. That is still a danger. A speaker can use biblical words, tell true stories about God and quote real principles, and still lead people into a practice Scripture does not support. Biblical vocabulary is not the same as biblical authority. Paul’s instruction is simple: “Test all things; hold fast what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:21). The Philistines also show that knowing true things about God is not the same as knowing God. Their acknowledgment of the God of Israel was real, but it did not make them His worshipers. When I weigh advice about God, do I weigh it against what He has said, or only against how spiritual it sounds?
items.q: When I weigh advice about God, do I weigh it against what He has said, or only against how spiritual it sounds?

sections.title: The Ark Comes to Beth Shemesh
sections.summary: The cows go straight along the road to Beth Shemesh, lowing as they go, and the reapers rejoice to see the ark. The Levites set it on the large stone, offerings are made to the LORD, and the narrator records the golden tumors and rats returned by the Philistine cities.

groups.title: The Ark Comes to Beth Shemesh

items.title: God Brings Himself Home
items.html: Across this section Israel does nothing to recover the ark. No army marches out, no priest goes to fetch it, and no one drives the cart. Two untrained cows walk a straight road, the enemy’s own lords follow behind, and the ark arrives in a field where people are reaping wheat. God brought the sign of His presence back to His people by His own initiative. That is the shape of grace. Jesus said, “the Son of Man has come to seek and to save that which was lost” (Luke 19:10), and John writes, “We love Him because He first loved us” (1 John 4:19). Salvation does not begin with our search for God. It begins with His coming to us. The people of Beth Shemesh only had to lift their eyes. The same God rules the circumstances we cannot steer. Two untrained cows did what no one could have made them do, while the lords of Philistia could only follow. Paul writes, “we know that all things work together for good to those who love God, to those who are the called according to His purpose” (Romans 8:28). That does not mean God approves every act that happens, or that the road will be easy. It means His purposes do not depend on our controlling everything. Before I took a single step toward God, He was already on the road toward me, and He is still directing the road.
items.q: Across this section Israel does nothing to recover the ark.

sections.title: Judgment at Beth Shemesh
sections.summary: The LORD strikes the men of Beth Shemesh because they looked into the ark of the LORD. They ask who is able to stand before this holy LORD God and send to Kirjath Jearim to take the ark.

items.title: Joy, Worship, Death, Fear
items.html: The second half of the chapter moves through four responses to God’s presence: joy at the ark’s return (v. 13), worship with offerings (vv. 14–15), the irreverence of looking into the ark and the death that followed (v. 19), and finally fear (v. 20). The day began with harvest gladness and ended with “the people lamented.” The joy was not the sin; the looking was. Yet joy did not protect them from treating holy things lightly. God’s presence is both a delight and a danger, and both are true at the same time. Scripture holds them together: “Serve the LORD with fear, And rejoice with trembling” (Psalm 2:11). A church can be warm, glad and full of energy and still grow careless about the holiness of God.
items.q: The second half of the chapter moves through four responses to God’s presence: joy at the ark’s return (v. 13), worship with offerings (vv. 14–15), the irreverence of looking into the ark and the death that followed (v. 19), and finally fear (v. 20).

whole.title: The Holy Presence Needs a Mercy Seat
whole.html:
Chapter 6 is framed by guilt and atonement. It begins with the Philistines trying to answer their guilt with a trespass offering of gold that their own priests devised (vv. 3–5). It ends with the men of Beth Shemesh struck for looking into the ark and asking, “Who is able to stand before this holy LORD God?” (vv. 19–20). In between, God’s holiness is the same whether the ark is in Philistia or in Israel. But the two peoples were not in the same position. The Philistines had no word from God and could only invent a remedy. Israel had what God had given: a priesthood, sacrifices of atonement, and clear instructions for approaching His holy things. Levites were there at Beth Shemesh to take down the ark (6:15). Their problem was not that God had provided no way, but that they did not honor the way He had revealed. The ark itself pointed to that way: over the tablets of the law God placed the mercy seat, where atoning blood was sprinkled. That covering was fulfilled in Christ, as the reflection at 6:19 explains. God’s presence is good news only for those who come under the atonement He has provided, and in Christ that atonement has been made once for all.

1 Samuel 6. The ark comes home, and God brings it Himself. The Philistines, who could only guess at God through priests and diviners, send it back with gold and a test they hoped might point to chance, and God answers in a way no one can explain away. Two cows walk a straight road, and the reapers of Beth Shemesh rejoice. But joy that grows careless with God’s holiness ends in lament, and the chapter closes with the question, “Who is able to stand before this holy LORD God?” God came near; His people were not yet ready to receive Him. The answer to their question is the offering God Himself provided in Christ.

What God may be saying: Perhaps something like this: I cannot get rid of my guilt by moving it, and I cannot satisfy God with my own remedies. He has provided the offering. He does not wait for me to bring Him home; He comes to me. And when He comes near, the right response is not to look on Him casually or to send Him away, but to rejoice with trembling and come close in the way He has made, the way of Christ.
whole.q: Chapter 6 is framed by guilt and atonement.

1.brief: The ark of the LORD remains in Philistine territory for seven months. The long stay shows how much the Philistines suffered under the LORD’s hand before they were ready to give up their prize.
1.explain:
“Now the ark of the LORD was in the country of the Philistines seven months.”

The narrator steps back to measure the ark's captivity. “The ark of the LORD” is still called the LORD's ark, even while it sits “in the country of the Philistines.” Its capture had not changed its owner. “Seven months” marks how long the Philistines held on to their trophy while the plague spread from city to city (5:6–12). The length of time shows how stubbornly they clung to their prize before they were ready to let it go, and how long the LORD's hand rested on them before they asked what to do.

hearing.observe: Seven months is a long time to keep something that is bringing God’s hand down on you. Ashdod had said, “The ark of the God of Israel must not remain with us” (5:7), and later the lords were told, “Send away the ark of the God of Israel” (5:11). Yet the whole episode stretched to seven months before the Philistines asked how to return it. The text does not tell us how long they waited after any one meeting, so we should not guess. But the length of the stay shows a people who knew what was crushing them and were slow to let it go.
hearing.hear: I can know that something in my life is under God’s hand and still hold on to it. I may tell myself I will deal with it, and months go by. The delay does not make it lighter. When the Lord shows me what I need to release, I want to yield early rather than carry for months a weight He never meant me to carry.

2.brief: The Philistines call their priests and diviners and ask what to do with the ark of the LORD and how to send it back to its place. The nation that captured the ark now wants only to be rid of it, and its own religious experts must find the way.
2.explain:
“And the Philistines called for the priests and the diviners,”

Having failed to solve the problem by moving the ark from city to city (5:8–10), the Philistines turn to their religious experts. “The priests” served their gods, and “the diviners” claimed to discern hidden things by reading signs and omens. These are the very practices the Law forbade in Israel (Deuteronomy 18:10). The counsel that follows comes from these men, not from the LORD, and it must be read that way.

“saying, ‘What shall we do with the ark of the LORD? Tell us how we should send it to its place.’”

The question has moved on since 5:8. The lords then asked what to do with the ark; now the people assume it must go and ask only “how we should send it.” They speak of “its place,” recognizing that the ark belongs somewhere other than Philistia. The nation that captured the ark as a prize now wants only to return it safely.
2.notes: The Hebrew word behind “the diviners” is related to the word Deuteronomy 18:10 uses for the forbidden practice the NKJV renders “one who practices witchcraft.” Both come from a verb meaning to practice divination.

hearing.observe: The Philistines called for “the priests and the diviners.” Diviners tried to read hidden things through omens and signs. Moses had told Israel, “these nations which you will dispossess listened to soothsayers and diviners; but as for you, the LORD your God has not appointed such for you” (Deuteronomy 18:14). In the next breath he promised, “The LORD your God will raise up for you a Prophet like me from your midst, from your brethren. Him you shall hear” (Deuteronomy 18:15). People who do not know the Lord are left to guess at Him. They read signs, consult experts and hope they get it right. The Philistines knew Israel’s God was dealing with them, but they had no word from Him, so they turned to divination.
hearing.hear: I do not have to guess at God. He has spoken, and He “has in these last days spoken to us by His Son” (Hebrews 1:2). When I am under pressure, it is tempting to look for signs, follow hunches or collect opinions, the way the Philistines called in their experts. Isaiah asked a people who were consulting mediums, “should not a people seek their God?” (Isaiah 8:19). Before I go looking for answers anywhere else, I want to open His word and ask Him.

3.brief: The priests and diviners advise that the ark of the God of Israel must not be sent back empty but returned to Him with a trespass offering. They acknowledge that their suffering is tied to guilt before Israel’s God, and they promise healing and an explanation of why His hand has not lifted.
3.explain:
“So they said, ‘If you send away the ark of the God of Israel, do not send it empty;”

The priests and diviners answer with a warning: the ark must not go back “empty.” They assume that the God of Israel has been wronged and that the wrong must be acknowledged with a gift. Calling Him “the God of Israel” shows they now see the ark as belonging to a God who has acted against them.

“but by all means return it to Him with a trespass offering.”

“By all means” stresses how necessary they think the gift is. “A trespass offering” is an offering that admits guilt and makes amends. The Philistine priests use Israel's own word for it, but the content of the offering will be their own design, not something the LORD prescribed. Their counsel confesses guilt before Israel's God without placing them under His law.

“Then you will be healed, and it will be known to you why His hand is not removed from you.’”

They promise two results: healing from the plague, and understanding of “why His hand is not removed.” The second phrase admits that the LORD's hand is still on them. Their confidence about healing is the claim of pagan religious advisers; the chapter will show the LORD's hand at work, but it does not endorse their method as a pattern for healing.
3.notes:
The Hebrew word for “empty” here is the same word used in the Law's command that no one appear before the LORD “empty” (Exodus 23:15).

“Trespass offering” translates the Hebrew word for the guilt offering, the offering Leviticus prescribes when someone has wronged the holy things of the LORD (Leviticus 5:15). Some translations, such as the ESV and NIV, render it ‘guilt offering.’

hearing.observe: These pagan priests did not call the plague bad luck. They knew the Philistines had wronged Israel’s God, and they knew something had to be given: “do not send it empty.” Guilty people feel that they must give or do something to make things right. Moving the ark from city to city had not solved anything, because guilt does not go away when we move it somewhere else. Their instinct was right, but their remedy was their own, and the chapter never reports that their promise of healing came true.
hearing.hear: I know that instinct. When I have wronged God, I want to do something to make up for it: try harder, give more, stay busy for Him. But my guilt is not settled by what I bring. It is settled by the offering God has provided. Isaiah says of the Servant of the LORD, “by His stripes we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5). So I can stop trying to pay, confess my sin honestly, and rest in what Christ has done.

reflections.title: Guilty People Want to Give Something
reflections.html: The Philistine priests did not call the plague bad luck. They told their people, “do not send it empty; but by all means return it to Him with a trespass offering.” They knew they had wronged Israel’s God by seizing His ark, and they knew something had to be given. That is how guilt works in the human heart. People who know they are guilty feel that they must give or do something to make it right. The instinct is true: guilt before a holy God does not disappear when we move it somewhere else, and during the ark’s seven-month stay in Philistia the Philistines moved it from city to city, but the trouble followed it. But the remedy was their own invention. The priests even promised, “Then you will be healed,” yet the chapter never reports that the plague ended in Philistia. A confident religious promise is not the same as a promise God has made, and a procedure that seems to work does not prove that God is behind it. The question is not whether I feel I must give something, but whether I am trusting what God Himself has said and provided. “He who covers his sins will not prosper, But whoever confesses and forsakes them will have mercy” (Proverbs 28:13).
reflections.q: The Philistine priests did not call the plague bad luck.

reflections.title: The Offering God Himself Would Provide
reflections.html: The Hebrew word for “trespass offering” is asham, the guilt offering Israel’s law required when something holy had been wronged (Leviticus 5:15). Isaiah uses that same word when he describes the suffering Servant of the LORD: “When You make His soul an offering for sin” (Isaiah 53:10). The Philistine priests promised, “Then you will be healed.” Isaiah says of the Servant, “by His stripes we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5). The priests sensed a true principle, that guilt before God must be paid for, but they could only guess at what might satisfy Him, and golden images could never pay that debt. God answered the need Himself. The golden tumors and rats are not a picture of Christ; the connection is the word and the need. What the Philistines could not provide, God provided in His Servant, Jesus. I do not bring God a payment and hope it is enough. I trust the offering He has already given.
reflections.q: The Hebrew word for “trespass offering” is asham, the guilt offering Israel’s law required when something holy had been wronged (Leviticus 5:15).

4.brief: When asked what the trespass offering should be, they prescribe five golden tumors and five golden rats, one for each Philistine lord, since the same plague struck the people and their rulers alike. The gifts are the Philistine priests’ own remedy, not a pattern God gave to Israel.
4.explain:
“Then they said, ‘What is the trespass offering which we shall return to Him?’”

The people ask for specifics. They accept that a trespass offering must be made, and they want to know what will satisfy the God whose hand is on them.

“They answered, ‘Five golden tumors and five golden rats, according to the number of the lords of the Philistines.”

The answer is gold shaped like their affliction: “five golden tumors” and “five golden rats.” The number five matches “the lords of the Philistines,” the rulers of the five chief cities (6:17). The gifts confess in visible form what the LORD had done to them. They are the Philistine priests' own remedy, not a pattern God gave to Israel.

“For the same plague was on all of you and on your lords.”

The reason for one gift per lord is that “the same plague” had struck everyone, rulers and people alike. No city and no class had escaped the LORD's hand.
4.notes:
In 6:4 and 6:5, as in 5:6, 9, and 12, the written Hebrew text has one word for “tumors,” while the Jewish tradition of reading the text aloud substitutes a different Hebrew word, possibly a less blunt term for the same affliction.

The Hebrew word translated “rats” is the general word for a mouse or small rodent. The KJV and ESV render it ‘mice’; the NKJV and NIV have “rats.” The Hebrew text of 1 Samuel first mentions these animals here, though 6:5 shows they had been ravaging the land.

hearing.observe: The offering was a confession in gold. Golden images of the very tumors and rats that had struck them said, in effect, “This is what Your hand did to us.” The priests also built a humbling fact into the gift: one of each “according to the number of the lords of the Philistines. For the same plague was on all of you and on your lords.” The rulers who had decided where the ark would go were under the same hand as everyone else. Their rank did not exempt them, and the offering itself put that on display. Peter learned the same truth centuries later: “In truth I perceive that God shows no partiality” (Acts 10:34).
hearing.hear: My position does not exempt me when God exposes something in my life. A parent, a pastor, a supervisor or a long-time church member can be tempted to think that responsibility puts him above correction. The lords of Philistia were counted with their people. When the Lord brings something to light in me, I need to face it as honestly as I would expect anyone under my care to face it, not hide behind my title.

5.brief: They tell the people to make images of their tumors and of the rats ravaging the land and so give glory to the God of Israel, hoping He will lighten His hand from them, their gods, and their land. Even pagan priests must admit that the God of Israel is the one pressing down on them, though they can only say “perhaps” He will relent.
5.explain:
“Therefore you shall make images of your tumors and images of your rats that ravage the land,”

The priests explain the gifts. “Images of your tumors” and “images of your rats” are models of the affliction itself. The phrase “that ravage the land” shows that the plague had struck the fields as well as the people. The Philistines were suffering both in body and in harvest.

“and you shall give glory to the God of Israel;”

The purpose of the gifts is to “give glory to the God of Israel.” In this setting, giving glory means openly acknowledging that He is the one who has acted and that He is in the right. Joshua used the same expression when he urged Achan to confess his sin (Joshua 7:19). The Philistines are admitting the truth about the God of Israel, though nothing in the chapter suggests they turn to worship Him.

“perhaps He will lighten His hand from you, from your gods, and from your land.”

Their hope is uncertain: “perhaps.” They cannot know whether the God of Israel will relent. “Lighten His hand” answers the description of His hand as “heavy” on them in 5:6 and 5:11. The words “from your gods” quietly admit that Dagon and their other gods had been struck as well (5:3–4, 7).
5.notes: In Hebrew, “glory” in this verse comes from the word group built on the idea of weight, the same group behind the LORD's hand being “heavy” in 5:6 and 5:11. “Lighten” is its opposite, from a verb meaning to make light. The priests hope that giving the LORD His due weight will make His hand light on them.

hearing.observe: In Hebrew the word for “glory” comes from a root that means “heavy” or “weighty.” For months the LORD’s hand had been “heavy” on Philistia (5:6, 11). Now the Philistines must give glory, give weight, to the God of Israel so that He will “lighten” His hand. In chapter 4 a dying mother cried, “The glory has departed from Israel” (4:22); here the people who captured the ark are told to give that glory back to Israel’s God. To give God glory is to tell the truth about Him and about ourselves. Joshua said to Achan, “give glory to the LORD God of Israel, and make confession to Him” (Joshua 7:19). The priests even admitted that God’s hand had been on “your gods,” remembering Dagon fallen before the ark.
hearing.hear: Giving God glory is more than singing words of praise. It means telling the truth: that He is the Lord and that I have needed Him to deal with me. I want to give Him that weight freely and gladly, not only when His hand is heavy on me.

hearing.observe: Notice the little word “perhaps.” The priests had no promise of mercy to offer, only a hope. Their religion could not tell them whether God would forgive. God’s people stand on something firmer: “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
hearing.hear: When I come to God confessing my sin, I am not standing on a “perhaps.” I am standing on His promise. I do not have to wonder whether He will receive me when I come honestly to Him through Christ. He has said He will.

reflections.title: The Light Burden in Place of the Heavy Hand
reflections.html: The priests hoped that if the Philistines gave glory to the God of Israel, “perhaps He will lighten His hand.” For months that hand had been “heavy” on them (5:6, 11). Jesus speaks to people who are weighed down: “Come to Me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest… For My yoke is easy and My burden is light” (Matthew 11:28, 30). The connection is one of theme, not of a shared word. Samuel’s “lighten” is a Hebrew verb and Jesus’ “light” is a Greek word, and Jesus is speaking of discipleship, not of a plague. But the contrast is worth dwelling on. The Philistines could only hope that the weight of God’s judgment might be eased. In Christ, the weight of judgment against sin has been carried, and He gives His people a different load, His yoke, which He calls light. Am I still carrying a weight Jesus has invited me to lay down?
reflections.q: Am I still carrying a weight Jesus has invited me to lay down?

6.brief: The priests warn the Philistines not to harden their hearts as Pharaoh and the Egyptians did, recalling that Egypt finally let Israel go after the LORD did mighty things among them. The memory of the exodus becomes a warning against resisting the God whose hand they now feel.
6.explain:
“Why then do you harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened their hearts?”

The priests reach back to the exodus for a warning. The Philistines had already spoken of the God who struck Egypt (4:8). Now their own priests use Pharaoh as an example of what not to do. To “harden your hearts” is to refuse to yield after God has made His power plain.

“When He did mighty things among them, did they not let the people go, that they might depart?”

Egypt resisted, but in the end the Egyptians “let the people go.” The priests' point is practical: resistance did not change the outcome for Egypt; it only multiplied Egypt's suffering. The Philistines would be wise to release the ark now. The LORD's “mighty things” in Egypt were still remembered by Israel's enemies centuries later.
6.notes: The Hebrew verb behind “harden” here means to make heavy. It is the same word group used for the LORD's heavy hand in chapter 5 and for Pharaoh hardening his heart in Exodus 8:15, 32.

hearing.observe: “Why then do you harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened their hearts?” The priests asked a simple question, and it showed how pointless resistance is. Pharaoh “hardened his heart” (Exodus 8:15) again and again, and in the end he let Israel go anyway. All his hardness did was add one plague to another. The words “harden your hearts” are literally “make your hearts heavy,” the same Hebrew root as “glory” in verse 5. A person can give God His weight, or make his own heart heavy against Him, and the second way never wins.
hearing.hear: Why do I harden my heart? When God is dealing with me, resisting Him does not change where He is taking me. It only makes the road longer and harder. Hebrews says to God’s own people, “Do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion” (Hebrews 3:8). If He is pressing on something in me now, the wise thing, and the kind thing for my own soul, is to give way early.

7.brief: The priests direct them to make a new cart, hitch two milk cows that have never been yoked, and take the cows’ calves home away from them. The arrangement is set against nature, since untrained cows would not ordinarily pull a cart or leave their young.
7.explain:
“Now therefore, make a new cart,”

The priests now give practical instructions. “A new cart” had never been used for ordinary work. To the Philistines this showed respect for the ark. It was not, however, the way God had told Israel to carry it. The Law assigned the ark to the Levites of Kohath, who carried the holy things on their shoulders (Numbers 4:15; 7:9).

“take two milk cows which have never been yoked, and hitch the cows to the cart;”

The cows are chosen to make the test difficult. “Milk cows” were nursing their young, and cows that “have never been yoked” had no training to pull a cart. Untrained animals would not be expected to pull steadily in one direction.

“and take their calves home, away from them.”

The final instruction makes the test harder still. With their calves shut up at home, the cows' natural instinct would be to turn back toward them. If the cows went away from their calves and toward Israel, the Philistines could not explain it as ordinary animal behavior.
7.notes: The Law also required certain sacrificial animals that had never borne a yoke (Numbers 19:2). The Philistine priests may have been following a similar sense that unused animals were fitting for sacred purposes.

hearing.observe: The priests built the test so that only God could pass it. Cows “which have never been yoked” would not know how to pull a cart, and nursing cows with their calves taken “home, away from them” would want to turn back. If those cows carried the ark away from home toward Israel, nothing else would explain it. The arrangement was the Philistines’ idea, not God’s instruction. But God chose to answer their test in a way no one could explain away.
hearing.hear: Sometimes God answers in a way that leaves no other explanation. I do not need to set up tests for Him, but I can recognize when He has done what only He could do. When that happens, I want to give Him the credit plainly instead of looking for some ordinary reason to explain it away.

reflections.title: The New Cart: A Reverent-Looking Method God Did Not Give
reflections.html: By pagan standards, a new cart and cows that had never been yoked showed respect. Things set apart from ordinary use seemed fitting for something holy. But God had already said how the ark was to travel: on the shoulders of the Kohathites, a clan of Levites (Numbers 4:15; 7:9). God brought His ark home on the Philistines’ cart anyway. They did not know His law. Years later, though, David copied their method: “they set the ark of God on a new cart” (2 Samuel 6:3). When the oxen stumbled, Uzzah took hold of the ark and died (2 Samuel 6:6–7). David afterward confessed, “we did not consult Him about the proper order” (1 Chronicles 15:13), and the Levites carried the ark “on their shoulders, by its poles, as Moses had commanded” (1 Chronicles 15:15). What God bore with from Philistines who did not have His word, He did not accept from His own people who did. A method can look reverent and still not be obedience. When I decide how to serve or worship God, have I asked what He has actually said?
reflections.q: When I decide how to serve or worship God, have I asked what He has actually said?

8.brief: The ark of the LORD is to be set on the cart, with the gold articles of the trespass offering in a chest beside it, and then the cart is to be sent off and left to go. No one will drive or guide it.
8.explain:
“Then take the ark of the LORD and set it on the cart;”

The ark is to be placed on the cart itself, not carried by people. The Philistines handle it as they think best, without the poles and Levitical carriers God had appointed.

“and put the articles of gold which you are returning to Him as a trespass offering in a chest by its side.”

The golden tumors and rats are to travel in “a chest by its side,” separate from the ark. They are described as “articles of gold which you are returning to Him,” an admission that the gifts are owed to the God of Israel.

“Then send it away, and let it go.”

No one is to drive or lead the cart. The words “let it go” leave its direction entirely to the animals, which is the point of the test. The phrase recalls the language of release from 5:11 and the exodus memory of 6:6.

hearing.observe: “Send it away, and let it go.” The Philistines did everything the plan required: they built the cart, hitched the cows, loaded the ark and the chest. Then they sent the cart away and let it go. The instructions named no driver. Whatever happened next would not be steered by them. In chapter 4 Israel had tried to direct God’s presence, carrying the ark into battle so that “it may save us” (4:3). Here the direction of the ark is left entirely to God.
hearing.hear: Some things I can do, and some things I cannot steer. I am responsible to do what God has plainly given me to do: work, pray, speak, prepare. But there comes a point where I have to take my hands off the reins and leave the outcome with Him. Peter tells me to cast “all your care upon Him, for He cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7). Entrusting a matter to God does not mean ignoring my duties. It means doing them and then letting Him decide where things go.

9.brief: The Philistines are to watch the cart’s direction: if it goes up toward Beth Shemesh in Israel’s territory, then the God of Israel brought this great evil on them, but if not, the plague was mere chance. The test is meant to settle whether the LORD’s hand truly struck them.
9.explain:
“And watch: if it goes up the road to its own territory, to Beth Shemesh,”

The Philistines are told to “watch” where the cart goes. “Its own territory” means Israel's land, and “Beth Shemesh” was an Israelite town on the border of Judah (Joshua 15:10).

“then He has done us this great evil.”

If the cart goes to Beth Shemesh, the Philistines will know that the God of Israel brought “this great evil” on them. The word evil here means disaster or calamity, not moral wrong.

“But if not, then we shall know that it is not His hand that struck us—it happened to us by chance.”

The test leaves room for another explanation: that the plague “happened to us by chance.” Even after seven months, the Philistines want proof before they will be sure the LORD struck them. The outcome will settle the question.
9.notes: The Hebrew word for “by chance” describes an event that happens without being planned or foreseen. The same word appears in Ruth 2:3, where Ruth “happened” to come to the part of the field that belonged to Boaz.

hearing.observe: After seven months of plague and a god fallen on his face, the Philistines still left a door open for “chance.” Unbelief always looks for another explanation. But Scripture says, “The lot is cast into the lap, But its every decision is from the LORD” (Proverbs 16:33). The Hebrew word for “chance” here is the same word behind Ruth 2:3, where Ruth “happened to come” to the field of Boaz. In Ruth’s story, what looked like chance was God’s quiet hand preparing redemption.
hearing.hear: When I look back over my life, I can see His hand in many things I once thought simply happened: a meeting, a delay, a door that opened or closed. What looked like chance was the Lord at work. That makes me more willing to trust Him with what I cannot understand yet.

hearing.observe: The priests called Israel’s land the ark’s “own territory.” In verse 2 they had spoken of sending it “to its place.” Even the enemy knew that God’s ark did not belong in Dagon’s land. It had been carried into enemy territory and set beside an idol in Dagon’s house (5:2), and it could not stay there.
hearing.hear: Have I carried God’s presence into enemy territory? Paul writes to believers, “what agreement has the temple of God with idols? For you are the temple of the living God” (2 Corinthians 6:16). I bring the Lord with me wherever I go. So I need to ask whether I have taken Him into places, habits or relationships where He is set beside idols. The Philistines knew the ark did not belong there. I should know that too.

10.brief: The men follow the priests’ instructions, hitching two milk cows to the cart and shutting their calves up at home. The conditions of the test are now fully in place.
10.explain:
“Then the men did so;”

The Philistines follow their priests' instructions exactly.

“they took two milk cows and hitched them to the cart, and shut up their calves at home.”

Each condition of the test is met: two nursing cows, hitched to the cart, with “their calves” shut up “at home.” The stage is set for a result that only the LORD's hand could explain.

hearing.observe: “Then the men did so.” The Philistines carried out every step their priests had given them: two milk cows, hitched to the cart, their calves shut up at home. They did exactly what they were told, though the advice came from priests and diviners, not from God. Israel, by contrast, had God’s word through Samuel in chapter 4, and the account gives no sign that anyone sought it before going out to battle (4:1).
hearing.hear: These men were careful to do what their advisers told them. Am I as careful to do what God tells me? It is possible to follow human counsel to the letter and treat God’s word as a suggestion. I want to take His instructions at least as seriously as these men took their priests’.

reflections.title: Careful Obedience to the Wrong Voice
reflections.html: “Then the men did so.” The Philistines followed their priests’ instructions to the letter: two milk cows, the cart, the calves shut up at home. Their advice came from priests and diviners, and they obeyed it exactly. Israel in chapter 4 had something far better, the word of the LORD coming through Samuel to all Israel (4:1), and the account gives no sign that anyone sought it before the army marched out. Chapter 4 does not record Samuel giving a command that Israel disobeyed, so the contrast is not between two broken orders. It is between people who did carefully what their advisers said and people who did not ask what God had said. Many people are careful to follow a doctor, a financial adviser or a coach, and casual about the word of God.

11.brief: They set the ark of the LORD on the cart along with the chest holding the gold rats and the images of their tumors. The ark leaves Philistia carrying the Philistines’ own confession of the plague the LORD sent.
11.explain:
“And they set the ark of the LORD on the cart,”

The ark of the LORD, which 4:4 describes as the ark of the LORD of hosts “who dwells between the cherubim,” now rides on a farm cart in Philistine country.

“and the chest with the gold rats and the images of their tumors.”

Beside the ark goes the chest with the gold rats and the images of tumors. The Philistines' own confession of the plague travels with the ark back toward Israel.

hearing.observe: The ark was the throne of “the LORD of hosts, who dwells between the cherubim” (4:4). Now it rides out of Philistia on a farm cart pulled by two cows, with a chest of gold beside it. The cart was the Philistines’ arrangement, not the way God had told Israel to carry the ark (Numbers 7:9), and the point here is not to approve it. The point is that God did not refuse to go home this way. The King whose throne the cherubim guard let His ark be carried on a farm cart. Centuries later Zechariah announced another King, “lowly and riding on a donkey” (Zechariah 9:9), and Jesus rode into Jerusalem that way (Matthew 21:5).
hearing.hear: God is not too proud to come to me in humble ways. He does not wait for a grand setting before He shows up. Paul says Christ “made Himself of no reputation, taking the form of a bondservant” (Philippians 2:7). If the Lord of glory was willing to come humbly, I have no reason to insist on being treated as important. I want to learn humility from the One who rode a donkey into Jerusalem.

12.brief: The cows head straight for the road to Beth Shemesh, lowing as they go and never turning to the right or left, while the Philistine lords follow them to the border. Against their instinct to return to their calves, the cows carry the ark home, and the LORD’s hand is unmistakably shown.
12.explain:
“Then the cows headed straight for the road to Beth Shemesh, and went along the highway,”

The cows do what untrained cows separated from their calves would not normally do. They head “straight for the road to Beth Shemesh” and keep to “the highway,” the main road, without wandering.

“lowing as they went,”

“Lowing” is the sound cattle make. The cows were crying as they went, a sign that their instinct still pulled them back toward their calves. They felt the pull of home but did not follow it. Nothing in their nature explains their course.

“and did not turn aside to the right hand or the left.”

The steadiness of their path is stressed. They “did not turn aside” in either direction. The LORD's hand guided animals that had no reason of their own to go to Israel.

“And the lords of the Philistines went after them to the border of Beth Shemesh.”

The five rulers follow the cart all the way “to the border of Beth Shemesh.” They become eyewitnesses that no one interfered with the test and that the cows went straight to Israel.
12.notes:
The Hebrew word for “the highway” describes a raised or built-up public road, a main route rather than a field path.

The expression “did not turn aside to the right hand or the left” is the same kind of language used in the Law for keeping exactly to the LORD's command (Deuteronomy 5:32).

hearing.observe: No Israelite army went to retrieve the ark. No priest went to fetch it. No one drove the cart. Two untrained, nursing cows went “straight for the road to Beth Shemesh,” away from their calves. The LORD brought the sign of His presence back to His people by His own hand. This is the heart of the chapter. It is also a picture of grace: God does not wait for His people to find their way back to Him. He comes to them. Jesus said, “the Son of Man has come to seek and to save that which was lost” (Luke 19:10).
hearing.hear: What a wonder that the Lord comes near by His own hand. He did not wait for His people to go and get Him, and He did not wait for me either. Before I knew to look for Him, He came looking for me. My walk with Him began with His initiative, not mine.

hearing.observe: Notice how the cows went: “lowing as they went, and did not turn aside to the right hand or the left.” They lowed as they went away from their calves, which had been shut up at home (v. 10), and yet they kept to the road. If, as many readers take it, the lowing was for the calves they had left behind, they felt that pull and did not give in to it. Christians have long seen in these cows a picture of costly, single-minded devotion, love for God above even the dearest ties (Matthew 10:37). Their road also brings to mind the road Jesus walked. He “steadfastly set His face to go to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51), and in the garden He prayed, “nevertheless, not as I will, but as You will” (Matthew 26:39). The cows were moved by God’s hand, not by faith, so the comparison is with the shape of the journey. But faithfulness is not the absence of feeling.
hearing.hear: There are times when obeying the Lord costs me something dear, and I feel it. Feeling the pull of what I am leaving does not mean I am failing. I can feel it, even with tears, and still keep walking His way without turning aside, as Jesus did on His road to the cross.

hearing.observe: “Did not turn aside to the right hand or the left.” That is the language Moses used for faithful obedience: “you shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left” (Deuteronomy 5:32). Two animals with no knowledge of God’s law walked the straight road that God’s own people had so often left. In chapters 2–4 Israel’s priests and people had turned aside. Here, under God’s hand, two cows did not.
hearing.hear: A straight path is possible when God’s hand is guiding. I am easily pulled off course by distractions, small compromises and what everyone else is doing. But the same Lord who kept two cows on the road can keep me on His path. I want to ask Him to direct my steps so that I do not turn aside.

reflections.title: The Highway
reflections.html: The cows “went along the highway.” The Hebrew word for highway here is mesillah, a built-up road. Isaiah uses the same word in his call to prepare for the LORD’s coming: “Make straight in the desert A highway for our God” (Isaiah 40:3). In 1 Samuel 6 the LORD brings His ark home along a highway. In Isaiah the highway is prepared for the LORD Himself to come to His people, and the Gospels apply Isaiah’s voice in the wilderness to John the Baptist preparing the way for Jesus. The narrator of 1 Samuel does not point to Isaiah, and Isaiah was written later, so this is an echo rather than a prophecy. But it is a fitting one: the God who brought His ark home on a highway is the God who came to His people in His Son.

13.brief: The people of Beth Shemesh are reaping their wheat harvest in the valley when they look up, see the ark, and rejoice. Their joy at its return is right and is not the offense that comes later.
13.explain:
“Now the people of Beth Shemesh were reaping their wheat harvest in the valley;”

The scene shifts to Israel. The people of “Beth Shemesh” are at ordinary work, “reaping their wheat harvest in the valley” below the town. The ark arrives without warning in the middle of harvest.

“and they lifted their eyes and saw the ark, and rejoiced to see it.”

When they look up and see “the ark,” their response is joy: they “rejoiced to see it.” After the loss of chapter 4, the return of the ark is good news, and their joy is right. It is not the offense that leads to judgment in 6:19.
13.notes: The wheat harvest was the season of the Feast of Weeks, which celebrated “the firstfruits of wheat harvest” (Exodus 34:22).

hearing.observe: The people of Beth Shemesh were not at worship or at war. They were reaping wheat on an ordinary workday. No one had gone to get the ark. They simply “lifted their eyes and saw the ark, and rejoiced to see it.” After the cry “The glory has departed from Israel” (4:22), this is a moment of pure gladness, and the narrator records it without a word of criticism.
hearing.hear: The Lord often meets His people in the middle of ordinary days. I do not have to save my gladness in Him for special occasions. Between one task and the next, I want to lift my eyes, notice His goodness and rejoice in Him.

hearing.observe: The ark was the place where God had promised to meet His people: “there I will meet with you, and I will speak with you from above the mercy seat” (Exodus 25:22). Christians have long seen in its homecoming a picture of God coming to dwell among His people. The ark is not Christ, but it points to the same desire in God’s heart that was fulfilled when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). His name is “Immanuel,” which is translated, “God with us” (Matthew 1:23).
hearing.hear: God wants to be with His people. That is not a small thing to me. The God who is holy and needs nothing has chosen to come near, and in Jesus He has done it in the fullest way. I can receive that with wonder, not as a doctrine to file away but as the reason I am never alone.

reflections.title: Wheat Harvest and the Feast of Weeks
reflections.html: The ark came home while the people of Beth Shemesh “were reaping their wheat harvest.” In Israel’s calendar, wheat harvest was the season of the Feast of Weeks: “you shall observe the Feast of Weeks, of the firstfruits of wheat harvest” (Exodus 34:22). Centuries later that feast was called Pentecost, and “When the Day of Pentecost had fully come” (Acts 2:1) the Holy Spirit was poured out on the believers. The text of 1 Samuel 6 does not mention the feast, and we should not claim the ark arrived on the feast day. But the season invites a quiet comparison. At wheat harvest God brought the sign of His presence back to His people, and at the harvest feast of Pentecost He gave His people His own presence by the Spirit.
reflections.q: The ark came home while the people of Beth Shemesh “were reaping their wheat harvest.”

14.brief: The cart enters the field of Joshua of Beth Shemesh and stops beside a large stone, and the people split the cart’s wood and offer the cows as a burnt offering to the LORD. The cart and cows that brought the ark home become an offering of thanks to Him.
14.explain:
“Then the cart came into the field of Joshua of Beth Shemesh, and stood there;”

The cart enters “the field of Joshua of Beth Shemesh” and stops. This Joshua is a local landowner, not the earlier leader of Israel. The cows stop by themselves, just as they had set out by themselves.

“a large stone was there.”

The narrator notes “a large stone” in the field. It will become the place where the ark and the gold are set down (6:15) and a lasting landmark (6:18).

“So they split the wood of the cart and offered the cows as a burnt offering to the LORD.”

The people use what is at hand. They split “the wood of the cart” for fuel and offer “the cows as a burnt offering to the LORD.” The cart and cows that brought the ark home become an offering of thanks to Him and will never be used again for ordinary work.

hearing.observe: The cart “came into the field of Joshua of Beth Shemesh, and stood there,” beside a large stone. The narrator does not tell us how it came to a stop, only where. The cows had set out with no driver named in the plan, and the journey ended in an Israelite field. The test the Philistines had set was answered from the first step out of Philistia to the last step in Joshua’s field. The ark came home the way God brought it.
hearing.hear: God finishes what He begins. Paul was “confident of this very thing, that He who has begun a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6). When I cannot see how the Lord will bring something to its end, I can remember the cart that stopped exactly where He meant it to stop.

hearing.observe: The people gave God everything that had carried the ark. They split the cart for firewood and offered the cows as a burnt offering, the offering that was burned whole on the altar (Leviticus 1:9). Nothing that had carried the ark went back to ordinary use. Read as a picture, the cows that went straight up the road, lowing, ended on the altar. Devotion that follows God’s way becomes a whole offering of oneself, what Paul calls “a living sacrifice” (Romans 12:1). The narrator reports the offering without pronouncing on every detail of it, so the point here is the people’s whole-hearted thanks, not a verdict that everything was done exactly as the law required.
hearing.hear: When I see how near the Lord has come to me, I want to give Him all of myself, not a part held back for ordinary use. This is not a demand pressed on me. It is what love does when it sees how much it has been loved.

reflections.title: The Carriers Became the Offering
reflections.html: The cows that carried the ark home did not go back to the field. They were offered “as a burnt offering to the LORD,” and the cart was split for the fire. What had carried God’s presence became the offering. Christians have long seen in this a picture of Christ. He came bearing the glory of God, “and we beheld His glory” (John 1:14), and then gave Himself as the offering: Christ “has loved us and given Himself for us, an offering and a sacrifice to God” (Ephesians 5:2). Some go further and see the wood of the cart as the wood of the cross. That is a devotional picture, not something the narrator says, and the cows were not willing as Christ was. The picture should not be pressed into a meaning for every detail. But the shape of the scene is worth holding: the One who brought God near to us is the One who was offered for us.
reflections.q: The cows that carried the ark home did not go back to the field.

reflections.title: The Field of Joshua
reflections.html: The cart stopped “in the field of Joshua of Beth Shemesh.” This Joshua was a local farmer, not Joshua the son of Nun. His name was common in Israel. Yet it means “the LORD saves,” and it is the Hebrew form of the name Jesus. The angel told Joseph, “you shall call His name JESUS, for He will save His people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21). The narrator gives the name no special meaning, so this is an echo for meditation, not an interpretation of the verse. Still, it is fitting that the ark came to rest, and offerings were made, in the field of a man whose name proclaimed that salvation belongs to the LORD.
reflections.q: The cart stopped “in the field of Joshua of Beth Shemesh.”

15.brief: The Levites take down the ark of the LORD and the chest of gold articles and set them on the large stone, and the men of Beth Shemesh offer burnt offerings and sacrifices to the LORD that same day. The ark is handled by those appointed to care for it, and the day of its return becomes a day of worship.
15.explain:
“The Levites took down the ark of the LORD and the chest that was with it, in which were the articles of gold,”

“The Levites” handle the ark. Beth Shemesh was one of the towns given to the priests, Aaron's descendants (Joshua 21:13–16), so men of Levi's tribe would have been present. The ark and the chest of gold are lifted down by those appointed to care for holy things.

“and put them on the large stone.”

They set the ark and the chest “on the large stone,” treating it as a fitting place to rest the ark in an open field.

“Then the men of Beth Shemesh offered burnt offerings and made sacrifices the same day to the LORD.”

The day of the ark's return becomes a day of worship. “Burnt offerings” were offered wholly to the LORD, and other “sacrifices” were made “the same day.” The town's first response to the ark's return is to worship.
15.notes: The account does not explain how the sacrifice of the cows in 6:14 relates in time to the Levites' lifting down the ark here; 6:15 may summarize what was done that day.

hearing.observe: The people “offered burnt offerings and made sacrifices the same day to the LORD.” Their first response to the ark’s return was worship. The joy of verse 13 turned at once into offering.
hearing.hear: When the Lord shows me His goodness, I want my gratitude to turn quickly into worship, the same day, not someday. Thankfulness that never becomes worship fades. Thankfulness offered back to Him grows.

reflections.title: The Ark in the Proper Hands
reflections.html: After its ride on a Philistine cart, the ark was taken down by “the Levites,” the tribe the LORD had set apart “to bear the ark of the covenant of the LORD” (Deuteronomy 10:8). Beth Shemesh was one of the towns given to the priests (Joshua 21:13–16), so Levites were at hand. The narrator makes a point of telling us who took the ark down. He does not describe every detail of how it was handled, and he does not pronounce the whole celebration correct. The burnt offering of verse 14 is one example: Israel’s law said a burnt offering from the herd was to be “a male without blemish” (Leviticus 1:3), and these were cows. The chapter does not name that as the reason for the judgment that follows; verse 19 gives a different reason. But the report is not a blanket approval either. Gladness and the presence of the right people did not make every part of the day obedient. Honoring God in the way He has shown is part of loving Him well. Grateful hearts still need to ask what He has said.
reflections.q: After its ride on a Philistine cart, the ark was taken down by “the Levites,” the tribe the LORD had set apart “to bear the ark of the covenant of the LORD” (Deuteronomy 10:8).

16.brief: After the five lords of the Philistines see the ark received in Israel, they return to Ekron the same day. They have witnessed the outcome of their own test.
16.explain:
“So when the five lords of the Philistines had seen it,”

The “five lords” who followed the cart have now “seen it”: the straight course, the joy of Beth Shemesh, and the worship. The test has answered their question.

“they returned to Ekron the same day.”

They go back to “Ekron” the same day. Ekron was the last city to hold the ark (5:10). The chapter records no change in their worship; they have witnessed the outcome of their own test and gone home.

hearing.observe: The five lords saw everything: the cows going straight up the road, the joy of the reapers, the offerings. They had their answer. It was the LORD’s hand. Then they went home to Ekron, and the text records no turning to Him. On the same day, in the same field, Israel worshiped and the Philistine lords walked away. Seeing God’s work, and even admitting it, is not the same as turning to Him.
hearing.hear: I do not want to be only a spectator of what God does. I can watch Him answer prayer, hear testimonies and even admit that He is real, and still go home unchanged. When He shows me His hand, I want to turn toward Him.

reflections.title: Witnesses Who Go Home
reflections.html: The five lords of the Philistines had seen everything: cows going straight up the road against their instincts, reapers rejoicing, offerings rising to the LORD. They had their answer to their own test. It was His hand. Then “they returned to Ekron the same day.” The text records no turning to the LORD. In verse 15 Israel worshiped “the same day”; in verse 16 the lords went home “the same day.” One day, one field, two responses. Seeing God’s work, and even admitting it, is not the same as turning to Him. Many people have watched God answer prayer, heard a testimony they could not explain, or felt His hand in a crisis, and gone home unchanged. Am I a witness of what God does, or one who turns to Him?
reflections.q: Am I a witness of what God does, or one who turns to Him?

17.brief: The narrator lists the golden tumors returned as a trespass offering to the LORD, one each for Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron. Every major Philistine city that suffered under His hand is accounted for in the offering.
17.explain:
“These are the golden tumors which the Philistines returned as a trespass offering to the LORD:”

The narrator pauses to record the offering in detail. The golden tumors were returned “as a trespass offering to the LORD,” the Philistines' acknowledgment of guilt before Him.

“one for Ashdod, one for Gaza, one for Ashkelon, one for Gath, one for Ekron;”

Each of the five chief cities is named. Ashdod, Gath, and Ekron had held the ark (5:1, 8, 10), but Gaza and Ashkelon are included too. Every major city under the Philistine lords is accounted for in the offering.

hearing.observe: All five cities are named, one by one, even Gaza and Ashkelon, which chapter 5 never says received the ark. The list reads like a record of tribute paid by a defeated people, written down so that the LORD’s victory would be remembered. Each city is named for its own share in the offering. The list does not tell us that anyone in those cities turned to the LORD. It records that each city had its part in acknowledging Him.
hearing.hear: A group response can hide an individual heart. I can sing with the congregation, stand with my family or agree with my church, and never make the response my own. Each city was named. “So then each of us shall give account of himself to God” (Romans 14:12). I want my answer to the Lord to be mine, not only the one I am carried along in.

18.brief: The golden rats match the number of all the Philistine cities under the five lords, both fortified cities and country villages, and the large stone where the ark was set still remains in Joshua’s field to the writer’s day. The plague reached the whole land, and the stone stands as a lasting witness to the ark’s return.
18.explain:
“and the golden rats, according to the number of all the cities of the Philistines belonging to the five lords, both fortified cities and country villages,”

The golden rats represent a wider area: “all the cities of the Philistines belonging to the five lords,” both “fortified cities” and “country villages.” The plague of rats had reached the whole land, not only the cities that held the ark.

“even as far as the large stone of Abel on which they set the ark of the LORD,”

The description reaches to the place in Israel where the story has arrived, “the large stone” on which “they set the ark of the LORD.”

“which stone remains to this day in the field of Joshua of Beth Shemesh.”

The stone “remains to this day,” that is, to the writer's day. It stood as a lasting witness to the ark's return and to what happened at Beth Shemesh.
18.notes: The NKJV's “the large stone of Abel” follows the traditional Hebrew wording, in which “Abel” may be a place name. The Hebrew words for “Abel” and “stone” differ by one letter, and many translations, such as the ESV, NASB, and NIV, read only a great stone or rock here; the KJV margin also gives ‘great stone.’

hearing.observe: The stone where the ark was set “remains to this day.” Scripture often marks God’s works with stones: Jacob’s pillar at Bethel (Genesis 28:18), the twelve stones from the Jordan set up “for a memorial” (Joshua 4:7), and soon Samuel’s stone called Ebenezer, “Thus far the LORD has helped us” (7:12). This stone marked the place where God brought the ark home, and it stood near the place where His holiness would be solemnly shown in 6:19. It called people to remember both His mercy and His holiness.
hearing.hear: I forget quickly. I want to keep reminders of what the Lord has done, both His kindness in coming near and His holiness that calls for reverence. Remembering keeps my heart grateful and humble at the same time.

reflections.title: A Stone That Remains
reflections.html: The narrator notes that the large stone where the ark was set “remains to this day in the field of Joshua of Beth Shemesh.” Scripture often marks God’s works with stones. Jacob set up the stone he had slept on as a pillar at Bethel (Genesis 28:18). Joshua set up stones from the Jordan “for a memorial to the children of Israel forever” (Joshua 4:7). In the next chapter Samuel will set up a stone and call it Ebenezer, “Thus far the LORD has helped us” (7:12). This stone marked the place where God brought the ark home, and it stood near the place where His holiness was solemnly shown in 6:19. It remembered both mercy and holiness. God’s people need both memories. Remembering only His kindness makes us careless; remembering only His holiness makes us afraid. What reminders of His faithfulness am I keeping where I will see them?
reflections.q: What reminders of His faithfulness am I keeping where I will see them?

19.brief: The LORD strikes the men of Beth Shemesh because they looked into the ark of the LORD, and the NKJV reports fifty thousand and seventy men struck, while some translations read seventy. The people mourn the great slaughter, learning that the LORD’s holiness governs Israel just as it governed the Philistines.
19.explain:
“Then He struck the men of Beth Shemesh, because they had looked into the ark of the LORD.”

The scene turns sharply. The LORD “struck the men of Beth Shemesh,” and the reason is stated plainly: “because they had looked into the ark of the LORD.” Their joy at seeing the ark in 6:13 was not the offense. Looking into it was. The Law forbade even the Kohathites, who carried the holy things, to look on them while they were being covered (Numbers 4:20). The ark was holy, and treating it as an object for inspection was a violation of that holiness. The LORD who humbled the Philistines also requires His own people to honor His holiness (Leviticus 10:3).

“He struck fifty thousand and seventy men of the people,”

The NKJV gives the number as “fifty thousand and seventy men.” Some translations read seventy instead, and the number is difficult in the Hebrew text (see Study Notes). On either reading, the judgment was severe.

“and the people lamented because the LORD had struck the people with a great slaughter.”

The people “lamented,” mourning “because the LORD had struck the people with a great slaughter.” They understood the deaths as the LORD's judgment, not an accident. The day that began with joy at harvest ends in grief.
19.notes:
The traditional Hebrew text reads literally ‘seventy men, fifty thousand men,’ an unusual way of giving a number. A few Hebrew manuscripts read only ‘seventy men,’ and the NIV follows that reading. Other translations keep the traditional text, as the NKJV does.

The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, reads differently in the first part of the verse, saying that some of the men were struck because they did not rejoice. The NRSV follows that reading. The Hebrew text followed by the NKJV states that they looked into the ark.

hearing.observe: The holiness that humbled Dagon and struck the Philistine cities was the same holiness among God’s own people. The Philistines suffered for treating the ark as a trophy. The men of Beth Shemesh suffered for treating it as a curiosity. God had said long before, “By those who come near Me I must be regarded as holy” (Leviticus 10:3). He was not being random or cruel. The reason is stated plainly, and His law had warned them.
hearing.hear: Belonging to God’s people never makes His presence something to handle casually. He is still God. I can grow so familiar with holy things that I stop treating them as holy. Paul warned believers about coming to the Lord’s Table carelessly: “he who eats and drinks in an unworthy manner eats and drinks judgment to himself, not discerning the Lord’s body” (1 Corinthians 11:29). I want to come to the Lord as one who knows Him and still fears Him.

hearing.observe: The same day began with harvest joy (v. 13) and worship (vv. 14–15) and ended with “the people lamented.” Their joy was not the offense; their looking was. Scripture holds the two together: “Serve the LORD with fear, And rejoice with trembling” (Psalm 2:11). Real joy in God and real reverence for Him belong together.
hearing.hear: I do not have to choose between gladness and reverence. My worship can be full of joy and still careful, warm and still humble. If my joy ever makes me careless with God, it has become something less than joy in Him.

reflections.title: The Holy Law and the Mercy Seat
reflections.html: Inside the ark lay the tablets of God’s law (Deuteronomy 10:5). Over the ark was the mercy seat, where the high priest sprinkled atoning blood on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:14) and where God promised to meet His people (Exodus 25:22). Read as a picture, the holy law apart from the covering God provides can only condemn. Spurgeon put it in one sentence: the law, when it is not covered by the mercy seat, is death to anyone. The narrator does not describe how the ark was opened, and he names the looking, not this picture, as the reason for the judgment. But the picture fits the rest of Scripture. Paul says God set Christ forth “as a propitiation by His blood” (Romans 3:25). A propitiation is a sacrifice that turns away God’s just anger against sin. The Greek word Paul uses is the same word Hebrews uses for the “mercy seat” (Hebrews 9:5). Christ is the covering God has provided. The only safe place for a sinner to come near a holy God is under the mercy He Himself has given.
reflections.q: Inside the ark lay the tablets of God’s law (Deuteronomy 10:5).

20.brief: The men of Beth Shemesh ask, “Who is able to stand before this holy LORD God?” and wonder where the ark should go from them. Their question rightly recognizes His holiness, but their response is to send His presence away rather than seek how to receive it rightly.
20.explain:
“And the men of Beth Shemesh said, ‘Who is able to stand before this holy LORD God?”

The survivors ask the right question: “Who is able to stand before this holy LORD God?” They recognize that the LORD's holiness is the reason for the judgment. To “stand before” Him means to remain in His presence without being destroyed.

“And to whom shall it go up from us?’”

Their second question shows their response: they want the ark to “go up from us.” Like the Philistine cities in 5:11, they seek to send God's presence away rather than ask how to receive it rightly. Their fear is real, but it pushes them away from the LORD instead of toward the obedience He requires.

hearing.observe: The men of Beth Shemesh asked exactly the right question. Hannah had sung, “No one is holy like the LORD” (2:2), and now a town feels it. Scripture keeps asking this question: “who may stand in His holy place?” (Psalm 24:3); “O Lord, who could stand?” (Psalm 130:3); “who is able to stand?” (Revelation 6:17). And Scripture answers it. No one can stand in his own right, but through Christ “we have access by faith into this grace in which we stand” (Romans 5:2). John saw a great multitude before the throne in robes made “white in the blood of the Lamb” (Revelation 7:14).
hearing.hear: Who can stand before this holy God? In myself, I cannot. But in Christ I stand, held in His grace and clothed in what the Lamb has done for me. That is the deepest security I know.

hearing.observe: Their second question tells a sadder story: “to whom shall it go up from us?” Like the Philistines before them, they wanted the ark gone, even though Levites were among them (v. 15). They did not ask how to receive it rightly. Feeling God’s holiness can lead us to come to Him His way, or it can lead us to keep Him at a distance. David later asked almost the same thing, “How can the ark of the LORD come to me?” (2 Samuel 6:9), until he learned to bring it God’s way (1 Chronicles 15:13–15).
hearing.hear: When I feel the holiness of God, I do not want to back away from Him. The gospel invites me to “draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith” (Hebrews 10:22). I want to come closer in the way He has made, not keep Him at arm’s length.

reflections.title: Who Is Able to Stand?
reflections.html: The men of Beth Shemesh asked exactly the right question: “Who is able to stand before this holy LORD God?” Hannah had sung, “No one is holy like the LORD” (2:2), and now a whole town felt it. Scripture keeps asking the same question. “Who may ascend into the hill of the LORD? Or who may stand in His holy place?” (Psalm 24:3). “If You, LORD, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand?” (Psalm 130:3). “Who can stand when He appears?” (Malachi 3:2). At the end, “who is able to stand?” (Revelation 6:17). And Scripture gives the answer. No one can stand in his own right. But through Christ “we have access by faith into this grace in which we stand” (Romans 5:2), and John saw a great multitude standing before the throne in robes made “white in the blood of the Lamb” (Revelation 7:14). The question of Beth Shemesh finds its answer at the cross.
reflections.q: The men of Beth Shemesh asked exactly the right question: “Who is able to stand before this holy LORD God?”

reflections.title: Holiness Felt, and God Sent Away
reflections.html: The second question of Beth Shemesh tells a sadder story: “to whom shall it go up from us?” Like the Philistines before them, they wanted the ark gone. The Philistines had said, “The ark of the God of Israel must not remain with us” (5:7). Pagan cities and an Israelite town both felt God’s holiness and both wanted His presence somewhere else. Beth Shemesh did not ask how to receive the ark rightly, though Levites were among them (6:15). Feeling God’s holiness can lead to repentance and a right approach, or it can lead to keeping Him at a distance. Holiness is uncomfortable to people who have not been cleansed. David later asked almost the same thing, “How can the ark of the LORD come to me?” (2 Samuel 6:9), until he learned to bring it God’s way (1 Chronicles 15:13–15). David’s fear turned into obedience, and the ark came to Jerusalem with gladness. The gospel does not answer God’s holiness by sending Him away. It makes sinners fit to come near: “let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water” (Hebrews 10:22). When God’s holiness makes me uncomfortable, the answer is not distance but cleansing. When I sense how holy He is, do I back away from Him, or ask how to come near in the way He has made?
reflections.q: When I sense how holy He is, do I back away from Him, or ask how to come near in the way He has made?

21.brief: They send messengers to the people of Kirjath Jearim, announcing that the Philistines have returned the ark of the LORD and asking them to come down and take it up. The ark that was welcomed with joy at Beth Shemesh is now passed on to another town.
21.explain:
“So they sent messengers to the inhabitants of Kirjath Jearim, saying,”

The men of Beth Shemesh send “messengers” to “Kirjath Jearim,” another Israelite town. Joshua 15:60 also calls the town Kirjath Baal.

“‘The Philistines have brought back the ark of the LORD; come down and take it up with you.’”

Their message reports good news, “the Philistines have brought back the ark of the LORD,” but asks the people of Kirjath Jearim to “come down and take it up with you.” The ark that Beth Shemesh welcomed with joy is now passed on to another town. It will remain at Kirjath Jearim a long time (7:1–2).

hearing.observe: The chapter ends unfinished. The ark is passed along to Kirjath Jearim, where it will be received with care (7:1) and will stay until David, the LORD’s anointed king, comes to bring it up (2 Samuel 6:2–3). The twenty years of 7:2 lead up to Israel’s lament; they are not the ark’s whole stay. Psalm 132 remembers that search for the ark: “We found it in the fields of the woods” (Psalm 132:6). Many interpreters take those words as a reference to Kirjath Jearim, a name that means “town of forests,” and the same psalm prays for the LORD’s “Anointed” (Psalm 132:10). Even when His people respond poorly, God keeps working out His purposes. The story of His presence among His people moves toward the anointed king and, beyond him, toward Christ, the Son of David.
hearing.hear: God’s purposes do not stall when His people stumble. Even when we push Him away, He keeps moving His story forward toward His King. That gives me hope for my own failures, and for the church’s. The King has come, and He will finish what He started.

reflections.title: The Ark Waits for a People and a King
reflections.html: The chapter ends unfinished. The ark goes to Kirjath Jearim, where it will be received with care (7:1) and will stay until David, the LORD’s anointed king, comes to bring it up (2 Samuel 6:2–3). The twenty years of 7:2 lead up to Israel’s lament; they are not the whole of the ark’s stay. Psalm 132 remembers the search for the ark, “We found it in the fields of the woods” (Psalm 132:6), words many interpreters take as a reference to Kirjath Jearim, “town of forests.” The same psalm prays, “Do not turn away the face of Your Anointed” (Psalm 132:10). Even when His people respond poorly, God keeps working out His purposes. His presence among His people moves toward the anointed king and, beyond him, toward Christ, the Son of David, in whom God has come to stay.

reflections.title: The Glory Comes Near, but Are We Ready?
reflections.html: Beth Shemesh rejoiced to see the ark and then sent it on to Kirjath Jearim. It is not enough for God’s presence to come near. His people must be ready to receive Him. Beth Shemesh had the joy of the ark’s return without the readiness to keep it rightly, and a people not ready for God’s presence will keep it at arm’s length. Israel would not be ready until chapter 7, when they lamented after the LORD, put away their foreign gods and returned to Him with all their hearts (7:2–3). The same is true for us. God may come near in a season of blessing, in a revival, or in a moment of answered prayer, and we may be glad. The question is whether our hearts have been prepared to welcome Him and keep Him, or only to enjoy the moment.
reflections.q: Beth Shemesh rejoiced to see the ark and then sent it on to Kirjath Jearim.
